common_name: Milton Sweetbay Magnolia (Extra Cold-Hardy Northern Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained-to-wet soil in full sun to partial shade; Milton's northern provenance makes it a good pick for gardeners at the cold edge of sweetbay's range, though it also handles Gulf Coast heat and wet soils without complaint.

directions: Set out container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring into consistently moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil, choosing a site in full sun to light shade near a low spot, rain garden, or pond margin where standing water is common after storms. Milton was selected from wild populations at the northern edge of sweetbay's native range along the Massachusetts coast, giving it noticeably better cold tolerance than typical seed-grown southern seed sources, though it performs equally well in the milder winters of zone 9a. Expect a multi-stemmed, loosely pyramidal small tree with silvery-backed leaves and lemon-scented, creamy white summer flowers, dropping some or all of its foliage in a hard winter before flushing back out in spring. Because it tolerates both boggy soil and periods of drought once established, it is a forgiving choice for the unpredictable moisture swings of coastal Gulf gardens.

common_name: Northern Belle Sweetbay Magnolia (Extreme Cold-Hardy, Large-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Northern Belle tolerates ordinary garden soil as well as boggy sites and shrugs off both hard freezes and Gulf Coast humidity.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it where consistent moisture is available since sweetbay magnolias naturally grow along streambanks and pond edges. Northern Belle was selected chiefly for its exceptional cold hardiness, but that same vigor and adaptability make it a dependable performer in the opposite extreme of Gulf Coast heat and humidity, forming a tidier, more tree-like upright oval than many seed-grown sweetbays. Its creamy white, lemon-scented flowers open somewhat larger than typical for the species from late spring through midsummer, and foliage stays semi-evergreen to evergreen in milder zone 9 winters. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood, and once established the tree tolerates both periodic flooding and short dry spells.

common_name: Santa Rosa Sweetbay Magnolia (Large-Leaved Gulf Coast Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist to wet, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Santa Rosa was selected in the Florida Panhandle and is exceptionally well matched to the heat, humidity, and sandy wet soils of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, acidic, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the tree ample room since it develops a broader, more spreading canopy than most sweetbay selections. Santa Rosa was introduced by Woodlanders nursery from a wild population in Santa Rosa County, Florida, and is distinguished by the largest leaves of any named sweetbay cultivar — glossy, leathery, dark green above with a bright white underside that flashes attractively in a breeze. Its fragrant, lemon-scented white flowers appear from late spring through summer, followed by the small red seed clusters typical of the species that draw songbirds in fall. Being sourced from the Deep South, it holds its evergreen foliage reliably through typical zone 9a winters and tolerates the swampy, seasonally flooded soils common in coastal gardens.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sweet Thing Sweetbay Magnolia (Dwarf Bushy Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sweet Thing's dwarf, dense habit fits foundation plantings and small courtyards where a full-size sweetbay would be too large.

directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sweet Thing tolerates more ordinary garden moisture than the species and does not require the boggy conditions typical sweetbays prefer. Patented as PP17,814 and discovered as a naturally dwarf, densely branched seedling, it matures as a shrubby small tree only about 8 feet tall and wide, far more compact than a typical seed-grown sweetbay, with slow, dense growth that makes it useful as a specimen, informal hedge, or large container plant on a shaded patio. Its cup-shaped white flowers, produced over a long stretch from early to late summer, carry a strong citrus fragrance and are followed by the small red seed clusters typical of the species. Light shaping after flowering keeps the naturally tidy, rounded form dense from the ground up.

common_name: Baby Doll Southern Magnolia (Dwarf Mounded Selection)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Baby Doll's wider-than-tall mounded habit suits it to foundation plantings and low screens rather than a narrow vertical space.

directions: Plant in moist to moderately dry, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, giving the canopy plenty of lateral room since Baby Doll spreads wider than it grows tall. This dwarf selection develops a dense, rounded to mounded form reaching only about 10 feet in height but 15 feet or more across, distinguishing it from the more upright, pyramidal habit of Little Gem. Large, fragrant white flowers open over a long season from summer into fall against glossy evergreen foliage, and because the seed set on this selection is sterile, propagation is done exclusively from rooted cuttings. Its low, broad silhouette makes it a good choice for a flowering privacy screen or specimen where height needs to stay in check but a wide evergreen mass is welcome.

common_name: Green Giant Southern Magnolia (Fast-Growing Gulf-Selected Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Giant grows quickly into a large specimen, so allow generous room away from structures and power lines.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing plenty of room since this is a full-size, fast-growing selection rather than a dwarf form. Patented as PP9,377, Green Giant was discovered as a seedling at a tree nursery in Selma, Alabama, and stands out among Southern magnolia cultivars for its unusually rapid, dense growth and its bold, coarse-textured, glossy leaves that stay green on both the top and bottom surface, lacking the rusty brown indumentum of cultivars like D.D. Blanchard or Bracken's Brown Beauty. The broad, blunt-pyramidal habit fills in quickly to make an imposing specimen or large-scale screen, and it produces the large, fragrant white summer flowers typical of the species once mature. Once established it tolerates the heat, humidity, and periodic drought of Gulf Coast landscapes with minimal maintenance beyond removing storm-damaged limbs.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
